questions.subject: Business Management SL
questions.syllabus_ref: Unit 4: 4.5 The seven Ps of the marketing mix (pricing strategies and price elasticity of demand); 3.3 Costs and revenues. Toolkit: descriptive statistics.
questions.subtopic: 4.5 A revenue-positive, profit-negative price cut: price elasticity of demand governs turnover, but contribution per member governs profit once a variable cost sits under the price
questions.challenge_mechanism: Every figure the manager offers is correct. The elasticity really is elastic, membership really does rise by a fifth, and revenue really does rise. The error is in what the decision turns on: an elastic demand makes a price cut revenue-positive, and says nothing about whether it is profit-positive once the variable cost of serving each member is deducted from the lower price. The item also removes the usual qualitative escape, because the membership needed to hold profit is well inside the gym's capacity, so "we could not fit them in anyway" is not available.

stimulus.title: A members' gym considering a price cut
stimulus.body:
Highfield Fitness is a single-site gym with a maximum capacity of $500$ memberships. It currently charges $£40$ per month and has $300$ members, so it is running at three-fifths of its capacity. The variable cost of serving a member is $£6$ per month, covering cleaning, utilities and consumables, and the gym's fixed costs are $£8{,}000$ per month, covering rent, staff salaries and equipment leases regardless of how many members it has.

The manager is concerned that the gym is not full and proposes cutting the monthly fee by $15\%$ to $£34$. A trial in a neighbouring town suggested that such a cut raises membership by about $20\%$, a figure the manager believes would hold here. The manager's argument is that revenue would rise because the gym would sell a fifth more memberships, and that this on its own makes the proposal worthwhile. The gym can admit up to $500$ members without any increase in fixed costs.

questions.question: The manager of Highfield Fitness wants to fill the gym by cutting the monthly fee, and argues that the extra memberships will raise revenue. Using the figures in the stimulus, calculate the present revenue, contribution and profit; calculate the price elasticity of demand implied by the proposal; show what the cut would do to revenue and to profit; determine the membership the gym would actually need to hold profit where it is; and evaluate whether the cut should be made.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the gym's current monthly revenue, its contribution per member, its total monthly contribution and its monthly profit.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the price elasticity of demand implied by the manager's figures, and state whether demand is price-elastic or price-inelastic over this price range.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Show that the price cut raises monthly revenue to $£12{,}240$ but reduces monthly profit to $£2{,}080$, and comment on why revenue and profit move in opposite directions.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Determine the number of members the gym would need at the new monthly fee to leave its monthly profit unchanged, and compare that number with the $360$ members the manager expects.

parts.label: e
parts.text: Evaluate whether Highfield Fitness should cut its monthly fee, referring both to the figures you have calculated and to the assumptions behind the manager's expectation.

questions.answer:
**(a)** Current monthly revenue:
$$300 \times \u00a340 = \u00a312{,}000 \;\; (A1).$$
Contribution per member is the price less the variable cost of serving that member:
$$\u00a340 - \u00a36 = \u00a334 \;\; (A1).$$
Total monthly contribution is $300 \times \u00a334 = \u00a310{,}200$, and after fixed costs the monthly profit is
$$\u00a310{,}200 - \u00a38{,}000 = \u00a32{,}200 \;\; (A1).$$
Note that the $£6$ per member is a *variable* cost: it is incurred only for members the gym actually has, which is why it is deducted from the price rather than lumped with the rent.

**(b)** The proposal changes the price by $-15\%$ and, on the manager's own figure, changes the quantity demanded by $+20\%$. So
$$\text{PED} = \frac{\text{percentage change in quantity demanded}}{\text{percentage change in price}} = \frac{+20\%}{-15\%} = -1.33 \;\; (M1)(A1).$$
The *magnitude* is greater than one, $|{-1.33}| > 1$, so demand is **price-elastic** over this range $(A1)$. That is exactly the condition the manager is relying on: with elastic demand, a fall in price raises total revenue. The candidate should be able to state that conclusion and it is correct.

**(c)** At the new fee the gym has $300 \times 1.20 = 360$ members and charges $\u00a340 \times 0.85 = \u00a334$, so
$$\text{new revenue} = 360 \times \u00a334 = \u00a312{,}240,$$
a rise of $\u00a3240$ a month on the $£12{,}000$ in part (a) $(A1)$.

Profit falls, however, because the contribution per member falls with the price while the variable cost does not. The new contribution per member is $\u00a334 - \u00a36 = \u00a328$, so
$$\text{new total contribution} = 360 \times \u00a328 = \u00a310{,}080,$$
and
$$\text{new profit} = \u00a310{,}080 - \u00a38{,}000 = \u00a32{,}080 \;\; (A1).$$
That is $\u00a3120$ *less* than the present profit of $\u00a32{,}200$.

Revenue and profit move in opposite directions because they are governed by different quantities $(A1)$. Revenue depends only on price times volume, and elasticity is precisely a statement about revenue; profit depends on the *contribution* each member makes, and the six-pound cut in price cuts contribution per member by the same six pounds, from $\u00a334$ to $\u00a328$, a fall of $17.6\%$. A $20\%$ rise in volume cannot offset a fall of that size in contribution per unit, so the total contribution falls even though the revenue rises. Elasticity is silent about profit because it works with revenue alone; the variable cost is what breaks the coincidence between the two.

**(d)** To hold profit where it is, the new total contribution must still be $\u00a310{,}200$, so the gym needs
$$\frac{\u00a310{,}200}{\u00a328} = 364.3 \;\; (M1)(A1).$$
Membership comes in whole numbers, so the gym would need $365$ members $(A1)$. The manager expects $360$ members, which is five short of the membership required, and at $360$ members the profit is the $\u00a32{,}080$ of part (c). The comparison to state is that the proposal misses its own break-even point by about five memberships, not that it is close to it: five members is a small number of people but it is the whole of the margin.

**(e)** On the figures given, the gym should **not** cut the fee. The decision is not close: every member the gym gains at $\u00a334$ adds $\u00a328$ of contribution, and the fee cut removes $\u00a36$ of contribution from each of the $300$ members who would have paid $\u00a340$ anyway. The gain from fifty more members (about $360 - 300 = 60$ extra, worth $60 \times \u00a328 = \u00a31{,}680$) is outweighed by the $300 \times \u00a36 = \u00a31{,}800$ given up on the members who were already there $(A1)$, and the two figures have been arranged so that this is exactly the $\u00a3120$ shortfall. A cut of this size cannot pay for itself unless almost every existing member stays and the new members arrive in numbers the trial does not promise.

The weaknesses in the manager's expectation should be identified rather than assumed away $(A1)$. The $20\%$ figure comes from a *neighbouring town*, so it is evidence about a different location, a different competing set of gyms and a different population; the manager's belief that it would hold here is an assumption, not a measurement $(A1)$. The trial also tells the manager what happened to membership when the price was cut elsewhere, with no indication of how long the effect lasted; a promotional price often attracts members who leave when it rises, which would raise the variable-cost base without building the membership the gym wants.

A judgement is required, and it should be a clear one $(A1)$. The strongest honest case for the cut is not in the figures but beside them: if the extra members raise the gym's utilisation, its classes fill, its atmosphere improves and its retention improves, then part of the benefit would appear *later* in lower turnover among existing members, which the item's numbers do not capture. That argument is real, but it is not what the manager offered, and it would have to be large enough to close a gap of at least $\u00a3120$ a month and probably much more. On the arithmetic presented, the recommendation is to keep the fee at $\u00a340$ and look elsewhere for the members: the gym has $200$ memberships of headroom and the cheapest way to fill them is not to reduce the contribution of the members it already has.
questions.markscheme_notes:
(a) (A1) for revenue $£12{,}000$, (A1) for contribution per member $£34$, (A1) for profit $£2{,}200$ (the total contribution of $£10{,}200$ may be shown as working). A candidate who treats the $£6$ as a fixed cost and deducts it after fixed costs will be wrong and forfeits the profit mark; the mark is for recognising that it is variable.

(b) (M1) for forming the ratio of the two percentage changes, (A1) for $-1.33$ or $-4/3$, (A1) for stating elastic with the magnitude test $|\text{PED}| > 1$. A candidate who writes $1.33$ without the sign and then calls it elastic has the substance and should keep the marks.

(c) (A1) for new revenue $£12{,}240$, (A1) for new profit $£2{,}080$, (A1) for the explanation that the contribution per member has fallen faster than the volume has risen. The explanation mark needs the per-member contribution, not "costs went up": a candidate who says only "revenue rose but costs rose more" without naming the $£28$ contribution has the first two marks and not the third.

(d) (M1) for setting the new total contribution equal to $£10{,}200$, (A1) for $364.3$, (A1) for rounding up to $365$ and comparing with $360$. Accept a candidate who works from the contribution lost on existing members and the contribution gained on new ones; the answer is the same. A candidate who answers $360$ because that is the forecast has not answered the question.

(e) (A1) for a reasoned recommendation against the cut, supported by the shortfall computed in (d). (A1) for identifying the transferability of the trial as an assumption. (A1) for identifying at least one further assumption (the duration of the trial's effect, or retention, or the absence of any change in variable cost per member). (A1) for a defensible judgement that weighs the qualitative case against the arithmetic rather than ignoring it. Full marks do not require the candidate to agree with the model answer: a clear case *for* the cut built on stated qualitative benefits, with the $£120$ gap acknowledged and argued, can score the fourth mark.

Forfeits: using $£40 - \u00a36$ as the new contribution per member after the cut, which double-counts the price change; computing elasticity from $£40$ and $£34$ directly rather than as a percentage change (that gives $-6/40 = -15\%$, which is the price change and no elasticity); stating the profit effect as positive because revenue rose. Condonation: contribution may be called "unit contribution" or "contribution per member"; $£2{,}080$ may be shown as $£2{,}080$ or "about $£2{,}100$" provided the exact figure appears once.
questions.explanation:
This item is built around the single most common error in pricing work, which is to answer a revenue question when a profit question was asked. The two are not the same, and the difference between them is a variable cost.

Price elasticity of demand is a statement about revenue, and it is a good one: if the magnitude is greater than one, a fall in price raises total revenue, and the numbers here are arranged so that this is true. The manager is not wrong about that at all -- revenue does rise, from $\u00a312{,}000$ to $£12{,}240$ a month. A candidate who stops at that point has done the elasticity correctly and has still given the wrong answer, because the proposal has to be judged on profit, and profit depends on contribution per unit, not on revenue.

The arithmetic that separates them is one line long. Cutting the price by $£6$ cuts the contribution of every member by $£6$, from $\u00a334$ to $\u00a328$; a $£6$ cut on $300$ members costs $\u00a31{,}800$ a month in contribution on the very members the gym already has, and the $60$ new members contribute $60 \times \u00a328 = \u00a31{,}680$. The gap is the $\u00a3120$ by which profit falls, and it is not a rounding error or a modelling artefact: it is the whole point. Elasticity could not have caught it, because elasticity compares percentage changes and does not know that the price has a cost underneath it.

Part (d) turns the same arithmetic into a target. The membership that holds profit is $31$ more than the forecast, so the proposal fails by five members, which sounds trivial and is not: the gym would have to reach $365$ members to stand still, and the trial it is relying on promises $360$. The distinction between "almost break-even" and "short of break-even" is the distinction between a project that should be reconsidered with better research and one that should be refused on the present numbers.

Only the evaluation part opens the qualitative door, and it is deliberately narrow. There is a genuine argument for the cut -- a fuller gym is a better gym, and happier existing members are less likely to leave -- but it is not the argument the manager made, and it does not appear anywhere in the figures. The mark is for noticing that the honest counter-argument rests on retention benefits the item has not quantified, and for refusing to let the assumption of a $20\%$ response from another town carry a decision worth more than the gap it has to close.

provenance.adaptation: Original. Price elasticity of demand is routinely taught alongside the rule that a price cut raises revenue when demand is elastic; the scenario here places a variable cost under the price so that the revenue conclusion and the profit conclusion diverge, and fixes the numbers so that the membership needed to hold profit sits above the forecast but below capacity.

difficulty_evidence.naive_path: Work out the price elasticity of demand from the twenty per cent rise in membership against the fifteen per cent cut in the fee, find a magnitude above one, conclude that demand is elastic so the cut raises revenue, and recommend the proposal on that basis.
difficulty_evidence.failure_point: Elasticity governs revenue and nothing else, while the decision turns on contribution per member, which the same six-pound cut reduces from thirty-four pounds to twenty-eight; a twenty per cent rise in a base of three hundred members adds sixty members worth one thousand six hundred and eighty pounds, which does not cover the one thousand eight hundred pounds of contribution given up on the members who were already there.
difficulty_evidence.wrong_answer: The recommendation is to cut the fee, justified by an elasticity of about minus one and a third, a rise in monthly revenue of two hundred and forty pounds, and the filling of spare capacity, with no calculation of contribution per member and no statement of the effect on profit.

verification.method: Every figure was recomputed from the stated price, variable cost, fixed cost and membership: revenue, contribution per member, total contribution and profit at both the present and the proposed price, and the price elasticity of demand from the two percentage changes. The membership needed to hold profit was obtained by dividing the present total contribution by the new contribution per member and was checked against the profit at 364, 365 and 366 members. The shortfall was cross-checked by computing the contribution lost on the three hundred existing members and the contribution gained on the sixty new ones.
solution_skeleton: work out the present revenue and the contribution each member makes after the variable cost
deduct fixed costs to obtain the present monthly profit
form the price elasticity of demand from the two percentage changes and test its magnitude against one
recompute revenue and total contribution at the new price and the forecast membership
solve for the membership at which the new total contribution matches the present one and compare it with the forecast

questions.subject: Business Management SL
questions.syllabus_ref: Unit 2: 2.1 Introduction to human resource management (workforce planning, labour turnover, absenteeism); 3.3 Costs and revenues. Toolkit: descriptive statistics.
questions.subtopic: 2.1 The cost of labour turnover against the cost of a retention pay rise, where the wrong comparison is total recruitment spend against total salary increase rather than the saving the proposal actually buys
questions.challenge_mechanism: The two headline figures are within six per cent of one another -- three hundred thousand pounds of recruitment and three hundred and fifty-two thousand pounds of salary -- and put side by side they invite the conclusion that the pay rise very nearly pays for itself. It does not. The three hundred thousand pounds is already being spent and does not change unless turnover changes; what the proposal buys is the sixty leavers it prevents, worth one hundred and fifty thousand. The numbers are also fixed so that no achievable fall in turnover can cover the increase: even a turnover rate of zero would save only three hundred thousand.

stimulus.title: A call centre weighing a pay rise against recruitment costs
stimulus.body:
Brightline Support operates a single call centre employing $400$ staff. The average salary is $£22{,}000$ a year. In the year just ended the labour turnover rate was $30\%$, and the finance function calculates that it costs $£2{,}500$ to recruit and train one replacement, covering advertising, agency fees, induction and the lost productivity of the new starter's first weeks.

The directors are worried about retention and propose raising pay by $4\%$ for every member of staff, from the start of the next financial year. The human resource manager expects this to halve the turnover rate, from $30\%$ to $15\%$, on the grounds that pay is the reason most leavers give in their exit interviews, and argues that a pay rise which halves turnover would save a great deal on recruitment and training. The directors have asked for the arithmetic before deciding. They have not asked about anything other than the effect on recruitment and salary costs.

questions.question: The directors of a call centre are considering a pay rise in order to keep staff. Using the figures in the stimulus, calculate the present turnover rate and the present annual recruitment cost; calculate the annual cost of the proposed pay rise; show what the pay rise would save and what it would add; determine how many leavers it would have to prevent to pay for itself; and evaluate whether the pay rise should be approved.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the number of staff who left in the year just ended, the present annual cost of recruitment and training, and express the turnover rate as it is normally stated.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the annual cost of the proposed $4\%$ pay rise across the whole workforce.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Show that if the pay rise did halve the turnover rate it would save $£150{,}000$ a year in recruitment and training, and that against its own cost this increases the call centre's total annual costs by $£202{,}000$.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Determine how many leavers the pay rise would have to prevent in a year in order to pay for itself, and compare that number with the total number of leavers at the present turnover rate.

parts.label: e
parts.text: Evaluate whether the directors should approve the pay rise, referring to the figures you have calculated and to the assumptions on which the human resource manager's expectation rests.

questions.answer:
**(a)** A turnover rate of $30\%$ on a workforce of $400$ means
$$400 \times 0.30 = 120 \;\; (A1)$$
staff left during the year. At $£2{,}500$ to recruit and train one replacement, the present annual cost of turnover is
$$120 \times \u00a32{,}500 = \u00a3300{,}000 \;\; (A1).$$
The turnover rate is already stated as a percentage of the workforce, so it is $30\%$; it may also be expressed as $120$ leavers against an average workforce of $400$, which is the same figure $(A1)$. It is worth noting that the $£300{,}000$ is money the call centre is *already* spending, not a new cost, and that nothing in the pay rise changes it except by changing the number of leavers.

**(b)** A $4\%$ rise on an average salary of $£22{,}000$ is
$$\u00a322{,}000 \times 0.04 = \u00a3880 \;\; (M1)$$
per member of staff per year. Across $400$ staff this is
$$400 \times \u00a3880 = \u00a3352{,}000 \;\; (A1).$$
The whole of that $\u00a3352{,}000$ is a new, recurring cost $(A1)$: it is paid every year for as long as the pay rate stands, and it is paid to all $400$ staff, not only to the ones the rise is meant to keep.

**(c)** If turnover halved, from $30\%$ to $15\%$, the number of leavers would fall from $120$ to $400 \times 0.15 = 60$. The saving is the cost of the $60$ replacements the call centre no longer needs:
$$(120 - 60) \times \u00a32{,}500 = \u00a3150{,}000 \;\; (A1).$$
The pay rise costs $\u00a3352{,}000$. The change in the call centre's total costs is therefore
$$+\u00a3352{,}000 - \u00a3150{,}000 = +\u00a3202{,}000,$$
a rise of $\u00a3202{,}000$ a year $(A1)$, not a saving. Put as totals: recruitment and training would fall to $60 \times \u00a32{,}500 = \u00a3150{,}000$, and with the new salary bill of $\u00a3352{,}000$ sitting on top of it the two costs together come to about $\u00a3502{,}000$ against the present $\u00a3300{,}000$ $(A1)$.

The essential point is which quantity changes. The present turnover cost of $\u00a3300{,}000$ does not become zero when turnover halves; it becomes $\u00a3150{,}000$. The proposal buys a *reduction* of $\u00a3150{,}000$, and it must be set against a cost of $\u00a3352{,}000$, not against the $\u00a3300{,}000$ that was being spent anyway.

**(d)** To pay for itself, the recruitment saving must equal the cost of the rise, so the number of replacements the rise must prevent is
$$\frac{\u00a3352{,}000}{\u00a32{,}500} = 140.8 \;\; (M1)(A1),$$
that is $141$ leavers must be prevented. But at the present turnover rate only $120$ staff leave in a whole year, so there are not $141$ leavers to prevent: even a turnover rate of zero would remove only $120$ replacements and save $120 \times \u00a32{,}500 = \u00a3300{,}000$, which is $£52{,}000$ short of the cost of the rise $(A1)$. The conclusion is sharp and worth stating plainly: on the figures given, the pay rise **cannot** pay for itself at any turnover rate, because its maximum possible saving is smaller than its cost.

**(e)** On the arithmetic, the directors should **not** approve the rise as a way of saving money, because it does the opposite: it adds $\u00a3202{,}000$ a year to costs even while delivering the halving of turnover the manager expects $(A1)$. The maximum saving available from the whole of the call centre's turnover problem is $\u00a3300{,}000$, and the rise costs $\u00a3352{,}000$, so the retention case cannot be made on recruitment savings at all -- the manager's mechanism fails before any assumption is tested.

The assumption should then be examined on its own terms $(A1)$. Halving turnover from $30\%$ to $15\%$ is a very large change to attribute to a pay rise of $4\%$, and the evidence for it is that pay is what leavers *say* in exit interviews; what people say when they leave is not the same as what would have kept them. A $4\%$ rise is below the level of inflation in most years, so it may not even be felt as a real improvement. If the manager is optimistic and turnover falls by less than half, the saving shrinks further while the $\u00a3352{,}000$ does not.

A judgement is still required, and there is an honest case on the other side $(A1)$. The figures only cover salary and recruitment, and the directors explicitly did not ask about anything else; turnover also carries a cost in service quality, in the loss of experienced agents, and in the morale of the staff who remain, none of which is in the $£2{,}500$ figure. If those costs are large, a pay rise could be justified as a *service* investment rather than a *recruitment* saving -- but that is a different argument from the one the manager made, and it would have to be supported by evidence the call centre has not gathered.

The recommendation should be direct $(A1)$. Approve no pay rise on the case as put, because the retention argument is arithmetically impossible: a rise costing $\u00a3352{,}000$ cannot recover more than $\u00a3300{,}000$ in avoided recruitment even if nobody left. If the directors want to reduce turnover, a smaller, targeted measure -- a retention bonus paid only to staff who stay, or an increase confined to the roles that actually leave -- would cost less than a rise paid to all $400$ and would not repeat every year for the staff it is not needed for.
questions.markscheme_notes:
(a) (A1) for $120$ leavers, (A1) for $£300{,}000$, (A1) for stating the rate as $30\%$. A candidate who gives $120$ and $£300{,}000$ without restating the percentage has the substance and keeps the third mark if the rate appears in the working.

(b) (M1) for the per-head increase of $£880$, (A1) for $£352{,}000$, (A1) for noting that it is recurring and paid to the whole workforce. A candidate who applies the $4\%$ to the $120$ leavers only, or to the recruitment cost, has misread the proposal and forfeits the marks.

(c) (A1) for the $£150{,}000$ saving, (A1) for the net increase of $£202{,}000$ (accept $£502{,}000$ against $£300{,}000$ as the statement of totals), (A1) for explaining that the comparison is against the *reduction* in recruitment cost, not the total. The third mark is for the reasoning, not the arithmetic: a candidate who computes both figures but writes that the rise "saves $£150{,}000$" without saying it costs $£352{,}000$ has not earned it.

(d) (M1) for dividing the cost of the rise by the cost per replacement, (A1) for $140.8$ or $141$, (A1) for the comparison with the $120$ leavers available and the conclusion that the maximum saving of $£300{,}000$ is still short. A candidate who answers "140 leavers" and stops, without noticing that only 120 exist, forfeits the third mark. The point of the part is that the target is unattainable.

(e) (A1) for refusing the rise as a cost-saving measure with the shortfall as the reason, (A1) for examining the assumption that a $4\%$ rise halves turnover, ideally with the observation that the evidence is what leavers say rather than what would have kept them, (A1) for identifying the costs the figures exclude (service quality, experience, morale of stayers), (A1) for a judgement that either proposes a cheaper targeted alternative or explains why the excluded costs could justify the rise despite the arithmetic. Full marks do not require the model answer's recommendation: a candidate who approves the rise on clearly stated service grounds, with the $£202{,}000$ acknowledged, can score the fourth mark.

Forfeits: comparing $£300{,}000$ with $£352{,}000$ and calling the difference the cost, which is the error the item is built to catch; assuming the whole $£300{,}000$ disappears if turnover halves; treating the pay rise as a one-off cost. Condonation: $140$ leavers instead of $141$ loses the second mark in (d) but not the first or third, since the comparison with $120$ is unaffected; the net figure may be given as $£202{,}000$ or $£200{,}000$ if the exact value is shown once.
questions.explanation:
The trap in this item is a comparison that looks natural and is wrong. Presented with a recruitment bill of $£300{,}000$ and a proposed pay rise of $£352{,}000$, almost everyone's first move is to set the two side by side, and the two are so close that the pay rise appears to be very nearly self-financing. The manager's case then seems to rest on the small gap, and the retention benefit is assumed to close it.

The comparison is invalid because the $£300{,}000$ is not what the pay rise saves. It is what the call centre is already spending, and it would still be spending a good part of it if the rise were approved, because halving turnover does not abolish recruitment; it halves it. What the proposal actually buys is the difference between two recruitment bills, and that difference is $£150{,}000$ against a salary increase of $£352{,}000$. This is the total-versus-marginal confusion in its most common business form, and it is worth more than the arithmetic that exposes it.

Part (d) then closes the escape that a candidate who has understood part (c) might still look for. If the pay rise falls short by $£202{,}000$, the obvious next thought is that a bigger fall in turnover would close the gap. It would not. The call centre has $120$ leavers a year; preventing every single one of them, which means a turnover rate of zero, saves $£300{,}000$, and the rise costs $£352{,}000$. The target of $141$ leavers prevented simply does not exist in a workforce that loses $120$ people. The proposal fails structurally, not marginally, and the difference between those two verdicts is what the part is for.

The evaluation mark sits on top of that. There is a real argument for paying staff more -- turnover damages service quality and drains experience in ways the $£2{,}500$ figure does not price -- and a good answer may make it. But it must make it honestly, as a service investment whose benefits are outside the arithmetic, rather than dressing it up as a saving the numbers refute. The stimulus is deliberately explicit that the directors asked only about recruitment and salary, so a candidate who invents other savings to rescue the proposal is answering a question that was not asked.

provenance.adaptation: Original. Labour turnover, its cost per replacement and retention pay are standard Unit 2 material; the item arranges those standard figures so that the total-versus-marginal comparison yields a confident wrong recommendation, and scales the rise so that no achievable fall in turnover can cover it.

difficulty_evidence.naive_path: Add up the annual recruitment and training cost of three hundred thousand pounds, compare it with the annual cost of the pay rise at three hundred and fifty-two thousand, observe that the two are close, and conclude that the rise very nearly pays for itself and should be approved for the retention it brings.
difficulty_evidence.failure_point: The governing variable is the fall in recruitment cost, not the recruitment cost itself, because the call centre already pays the three hundred thousand and keeps paying most of it; the rise prevents sixty of the one hundred and twenty leavers and so saves one hundred and fifty thousand against a cost of three hundred and fifty-two thousand, and even the impossible case of no leavers saves only three hundred thousand.
difficulty_evidence.wrong_answer: The recommendation is to approve the pay rise on the grounds that recruitment costs of three hundred thousand pounds are almost as large as the salary increase of three hundred and fifty-two thousand, so the two nearly cancel and the retention benefit decides the question.

verification.method: The number of leavers, the recruitment bill, the per-head and total cost of the rise and the recruitment saving were each recomputed from the stated figures, and all four were checked against each other for consistency. The unattainability of the payback was confirmed twice, once by dividing the cost of the rise by the cost per replacement to obtain 140.8, and once by computing the largest possible saving at a turnover rate of zero and comparing it with the cost of the rise.
solution_skeleton: apply the turnover rate to the workforce to obtain the number of leavers and cost the replacements
apply the percentage rise to the average salary and scale it across the whole workforce
cost the replacements that would be avoided if turnover halved and set that against the rise
solve for the number of leavers that would pay for the rise and compare it with the number that exist
separate the arithmetic verdict from the benefits the figures do not contain
